Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

false_positives.candidate:
N+1 free pattern but new repository instance ignores credential type correctness

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds is called with all credentialIds including non-Google-calendar integrations (Office365, etc.) and in-memory delegation credentials whose credentialId may be negative (per isInMemoryDelegationCredential checks elsewhere in CalendarCacheRepository). Passing negative/in-memory credential IDs into the groupBy query is harmless but wasteful, and more importantly it does not filter by integration type, so the resulting cacheUpdatedAt map is computed for all credential types though it's only meaningful for Google Calendar. This doesn't match the pattern elsewhere in the code (e.g. assertCalendarHasDbCredential) which explicitly guards against invalid credential ids being used in cache lookups.

Unconditional updateManyByCredentialId call after every fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache regardless of cache miss/hit

fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache now unconditionally calls SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId for all selected calendars under the credential, bumping SelectedCalendar.updatedAt even when this method is invoked as part of routine operations (e.g., unwatchCalendar's call to repopulate cache for remaining calendars). This adds an extra DB write on every fetch cycle, which, combined with CalendarCache being queried heavily, could add non-trivial write load, and the PR description itself notes this field isn't actually surfaced in the UI (cacheUpdatedAt from CalendarCache is used instead), making this update likely unnecessary overhead.

deleteCache does not check delegation credential ownership

The handler only looks up prisma.credential with userId filter. For delegation credentials (which may not have a direct userId or are shared), this check could incorrectly allow or deny access, or miss validating that the credential actually belongs to the acting user in multi-tenant/org scenarios. Other handlers in this codebase use more thorough credential ownership checks (including org/team credentials). This bypass could allow deleting cache for credentials not truly owned by the user if credential.userId semantics differ (e.g., shared/team credentials).

interpolation option improperly placed inside t() call

The `interpolation: { escapeValue: false }` option is passed inside the same object as the `timestamp` interpolation value for `t("cache_last_updated", {...})`. react-i18next expects interpolation options to be passed separately (as part of i18next options), not mixed with variables; here it will be treated as an extra named variable, not as an actual interpolation config, so it has no effect and could show up unexpectedly if the translation string references it.

updatedAt added as @updatedAt but migration lacks backfill/default consistency check

The Prisma field uses @default(now()) @updatedAt, meaning Prisma manages it automatically on every write (including raw upsert calls in calendar-cache.repository.ts that don't explicitly set updatedAt). This is fine for Prisma Client writes, but any raw SQL inserts/updates to CalendarCache (e.g. via migrations or external scripts) that don't go through Prisma Client will not get updatedAt refreshed automatically, since @updatedAt is implemented at Prisma Client/query level, not DB level. If any other code path writes to CalendarCache via raw queries, cache status reporting will be stale/incorrect.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach with async callback is not awaited, breaking error handling and ordering

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...}) is used inside a try/catch block. Array.prototype.forEach does not wait for async callbacks, so any error thrown inside the async callback (including from the newly-async getCalendar call) becomes an unhandled promise rejection rather than being caught by the surrounding try/catch. Additionally, the outer function can proceed (e.g. to sending emails) before calendar/video deletions actually complete, since forEach doesn't return a promise. This should use Promise.all with .map instead of forEach.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic import() at module top-level still eagerly loads every app at startup

The appStore object's values are the results of calling import("./appX") directly as object literal properties. These import() calls execute immediately when the appStore module is evaluated (object literals evaluate all their values eagerly), so every app package is still loaded eagerly at process startup, exactly as before, just now wrapped in Promises. This defeats the stated purpose of the PR (async/lazy imports) while adding await overhead at every call site (getCalendar, getVideoAdapters, payment app lookups, etc.) without actually deferring any loading or enabling code splitting benefits. A lazy factory, e.g. appStore[app] as a function returning import(...), would be needed to truly delay loading until first use.

Same forEach(async ...) issue as vital/reschedule.ts

Identical to the vital reschedule.ts issue: bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...}) inside try/catch does not propagate errors into the catch block and does not block execution until the async deleteEvent/deleteMeeting calls resolve, since getCalendar is now async. This can silently swallow calendar/video deletion failures and proceed to send reschedule emails before cleanup finishes.

forEach(async ...) means booking cancellation side effects are not awaited

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... }) is not awaited by the caller. Since getCalendar is now async, the loop fires off promises that are not tracked, so sendRequestRescheduleEmail and the webhook dispatch further down can run before the calendar/video deletions complete, and any errors from these async calls become unhandled rejections instead of being surfaced.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
workingHours check compares start==end, always false condition

In checkIfIsAvailable, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` duplicates the computation of `start` instead of using slotEndTime. This makes the working-hours boundary check (`end > workingHour.endTime`) effectively check the slot start time twice instead of validating the slot's end time against working hours, so slots that end after working hours but start within them will incorrectly be considered available.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs object comparison with === never true

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two different Dayjs object instances with strict equality, which is always false since Dayjs objects are not primitives. This dead code branch (meant to detect override start===end, i.e. an all-day-unavailable override) never triggers, so overrides representing a fully blocked day won't be handled as intended.

false_positives.candidate:
No test coverage for round-robin + date override interaction

The PR's primary claimed fix is that fixed-host date overrides are respected in round-robin events, but no test in this file exercises a round-robin event type combined with a date override for a fixed host. Only the plain date-override timezone case and existing round-robin busy-time tests are covered, leaving the main bug fix for issue #8207 unverified by tests.

Override's own date may shift when offset computed relative to invitee tz with DST mismatch

The override startTime/endTime are computed as `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset,'minute')` where offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset. However `organizerUtcOffset` is derived from `override.start` parsed with `dayjs(override.start.toString())` rather than from the already-known override.timeZone-based organizer time directly; if `override.start` lacks timezone info (just a date string), `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` may misinterpret the local wall time, causing an incorrect offset and shifted slot times for overrides near DST transitions.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
CSRF/replay: state reused from pipeline.signature without binding to session nonce

The state check compares `request.GET.get('state')` directly to `pipeline.signature`, which is a deterministic value derived from pipeline state rather than a per-session random nonce. If an attacker can predict or capture this signature (e.g., via logs, referrer leakage, or by initiating their own pipeline with similar session state), they could craft a matching callback to replay or cross-link an OAuth flow. Typically CSRF-state tokens should be freshly generated random values stored server-side and compared, not a reproducible signature of pipeline data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError risk if integration.metadata lacks 'sender'

`integration.metadata['sender']['login']` is accessed directly without checking existence. If an installation's metadata doesn't contain a 'sender' key (e.g., legacy integrations installed before this feature, or integrations created via other paths), this raises a KeyError instead of gracefully failing with the intended `error()` response, causing an unhandled 500 instead of a user-friendly error page.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing

false_positives.candidate:
Hardcoded provider_id check reduces extensibility without clear doc

Replacing the list-based `FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR` constant with an inline string literal check (`provider_id == 'github'`) removes the previous extension point for other providers needing the same install-redirect behavior; if another provider needs similar handling in the future, this requires modifying this file directly rather than extending a configurable list, which was arguably better practice given multiple pipeline-based integrations exist.

No validation of error/exception responses from token exchange and user info calls

`safe_urlopen`/`safe_urlread` and `get_user_info` calls are wrapped only loosely: body parsing failures fall back to an empty dict silently (bare except swallowing all exceptions), and `get_user_info` is called without any try/except — if GitHub returns a non-200 or malformed response, `get_user_info` could raise an unhandled exception (e.g., ApiError) instead of being caught and converted to a friendly `error()` response, resulting in a raw 500 to the user instead of the intended integration-failed page.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Default datetime evaluated once at class definition time

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass default evaluated once when the module is loaded, not per-instance. All AssignmentSource instances created without explicitly passing `queued` will share the same stale timestamp (the time the module was imported), not the time the instance was created. This should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.
to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

false_positives.candidate:
Sync-cycle check compares integration_id to org_integration.integration_id but AssignmentSource is built from models.Integration without currently-synced-integration disambiguation

`should_sync` only guards against the same integration that originated the change; it does not persist/propagate the assignment_source through intermediate inbound sync tasks (e.g. `sync_status_inbound`), so chains of different sync types between the same integration are not fully protected, and other call sites (e.g. status sync inbound task) are not shown to pass assignment_source consistently, risking partial fixes for the described loop.

where_should_sync does not pass sync_source to should_sync

In `where_should_sync`, `installation.should_sync(key)` is called without a `sync_source` argument, so this path never benefits from the new assignment-source cycle-breaking logic. If this function is used anywhere relevant to assignment sync, cycles could still occur through this code path.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstractmethod build_occurrence_and_event_data breaks existing non-stateful DetectorHandler subclasses only partially

Adding @abc.abstractmethod build_occurrence_and_event_data to StatefulDetectorHandler is a breaking API change for all existing subclasses of StatefulDetectorHandler that don't implement this method; they will fail to instantiate. The PR only updates grouptype.py's MetricAlertDetectorHandler (which doesn't implement it either, so it will raise TypeError when instantiated), and the test's MockDetectorStateHandler. Any other subclasses in the codebase not shown here (or added later) will break without a clear error message tied to this specific hook; the TODO comment in grouptype.py doesn't mention this requirement for implementers.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.

Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

false_positives.candidate:
Removed duplicate group_key detection without replacement safeguard

The previous process_detectors logic explicitly checked for duplicate group_keys from detector_results and logged an error, skipping duplicates. Now that evaluate returns a dict keyed by group_key, duplicates are implicitly deduped by dict insertion order, silently overwriting the first result without any logging or metric. This removes an existing data-integrity safeguard/signal that previously surfaced bugs in detector implementations producing colliding group keys; now such bugs will fail silently (lost occurrence) instead of being logged.

evaluate_group_key_value calls build_occurrence_and_event_data with raw value, not necessarily matching group_key's current value semantics

In evaluate_group_key_value, build_occurrence_and_event_data is called with 'value' (the raw metric value for this evaluation), but the abstract method's signature/docstring doesn't clarify units or validate correctness. If a subclass's new_status is e.g. OK transitioning to non-OK, the value passed may not correspond to what caused the status change if multiple conditions were evaluated across different value representations. This is minor but could confuse implementers producing occurrence evidence.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() deadline handling can let a process be killed/skipped silently without raising

In join(), the loop `for process_index, process in self.processes.items(): if deadline is not None: remaining_time = deadline - time.time(); if remaining_time <= 0: break` just breaks out of the whole loop once the deadline is exceeded for any single process, leaving the remaining processes neither waited-on nor terminated. Previously there was only one process so this corner case didn't exist; now, with multiple processes, some may be left running (not terminated) if the deadline is hit partway through, leaking subprocesses after shutdown of the strategy pipeline step and continuing to write to Kafka/Redis after the main process intends to be done with this instance's lifecycle (e.g. during rebalance restarts) causing duplicate/zombie flusher activity until the whole consumer process exits.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

false_positives.candidate:
Each sub-flusher process creates its own separate SpansBuffer and Redis connections

_create_process_for_shards creates a new SpansBuffer(shards) per process and multiple processes now share the same backing Redis, but each gets its own connection pool / client. With many processes per consumer (num_processes shards split across up to flusher_processes), this multiplies Redis connections significantly beyond what one buffer-per-consumer used before, which can exhaust Redis maxclients under scale-up scenarios the PR is explicitly targeting (scaling down consumers but relying on more flusher processes).

max_processes default silently falls back to shard count causing non-deterministic process count across runs with varying partitions

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` means if `max_processes=0` is passed, it is treated as falsy and replaced by shard count, which could be surprising/undocumented behavior (0 should probably mean "zero processes" or raise, not fall back silently). This isn't tested and could mask configuration bugs where `flusher_processes=0` is passed unintentionally via CLI defaulting weirdly.

process.kill() only guarded for multiprocessing.Process, silently no-ops for Thread

In _ensure_processes_alive, `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` means that when running in testing mode where processes are threading.Thread (produce_to_pipe set), an unhealthy/dead thread is never killed (threads can't be killed) but also _create_process_for_shards is still called to spawn a replacement, potentially leaving the old hung thread running indefinitely alongside the new one, leading to duplicate flush activity in tests using produce_to_pipe mode if a thread were ever detected unhealthy.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
OffsetTracker.all_offsets dict grows unbounded for low-traffic partitions

`get_committable_offsets()` iterates `self.all_offsets.keys()` but never removes a partition's entry when its offset set becomes empty (it is only pruned in `mark_committed`, which filters by offset value, not deleting the partition key entirely when offsets are completed without any commit happening, e.g. for FilteredPayload offsets added+completed immediately). Over the life of a long-running consumer process this results in slow unbounded growth of `all_offsets`/`outstanding`/`partition_locks` dictionaries, particularly for partitions that get reassigned/rebalanced repeatedly, since partition keys are never fully removed.

Per-message metrics.gauge call on queue depth may add significant overhead

`OrderedQueueWorker.run()` emits a `metrics.gauge` call for every processed item (line 150-156), tagged by identifier. For high-throughput queues (e.g. uptime results) this adds a statsd/metrics emission per message per worker, which may become a non-trivial source of overhead/metrics volume at scale, especially compared to the previous batch-based processing which could emit stats per batch rather than per item.

Use of queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown() requires Python 3.13+

The code relies on `queue.ShutDown` (as an exception type) and `queue.Queue.shutdown()` (lines 132, 142, 238), both of which were only added to the stdlib `queue` module in Python 3.13. Sentry currently targets Python 3.11/3.12, so `queue.Queue` instances will not have a `shutdown()` method and `queue.ShutDown` will raise `AttributeError` when referenced. In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` (line 238) the `AttributeError` is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` and merely logged, meaning the queue is never actually shut down and the worker threads remain blocked forever on `work_queue.get()` since they have no timeout and no sentinel value to unblock them. This leaves daemon threads running indefinitely (though daemon threads won't block process exit, `join(timeout=5.0)` will always time out and `thread-queue-parallel` mode will never cleanly release workers), and the whole feature is effectively broken/untested on the Python version this repo runs.

Worker threads block forever on queue.get() with no way to interrupt on unsupported Python versions

`OrderedQueueWorker.run()` calls `self.work_queue.get()` with no timeout, relying entirely on `queue.ShutDown` being raised by `Queue.shutdown()` to break out of the loop during shutdown. Since this stdlib behavior doesn't exist before Python 3.13 (see above), setting `self.shutdown = True` has no effect on an already-blocked `.get()` call — the thread will never notice the shutdown flag unless a new item arrives. This means on consumer shutdown, worker threads can hang, and `strategy.close()`/`terminate()` won't actually stop in-flight work promptly, risking data loss or delayed shutdown during deploys.

num_queues defaults to max_workers but worker count semantics changed silently

In `thread-queue-parallel` mode, `max_workers` (previously documented as thread pool size for `batched-parallel`) is reused to mean "number of fixed queues" (`num_queues=max_workers or 20`). Each queue spawns exactly one dedicated worker thread for its lifetime (in `FixedQueuePool.__init__`), so unlike `batched-parallel`'s ThreadPoolExecutor (which dynamically allocates threads bounded by max_workers), this always creates `num_queues` persistent threads regardless of actual load. This is a meaningful behavior change for the same CLI option across modes, worth documenting more clearly, especially since the click help text for `--max-workers` was only updated to "maximum amount of parallelism" without noting the always-on persistent threads per queue in this mode.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache never invalidated on permission changes, risking stale denies

permDenialCache entries are set with a TTL (shortCacheTTL=30s) but are never explicitly invalidated when a user's permissions change (e.g. after a grant). Although the TTL will eventually expire the entry, during that window a user who is just granted access to a resource (e.g. the folder/dashboard they just created) could still be denied if a prior Check attempt cached a denial for the exact same name/action/parent combination before the permission was granted. This can reintroduce the very bug this PR aims to fix (can't access just-created resources) in edge cases where Check is called before creation completes and then re-checked within the TTL window.

In-proc server still uses a 5 minute local cache for all cache wraps including the new denial cache

In ProvideAuthZClient, the Service is constructed with a single shared cache.NewLocalCache(cache.Config{Expiry: 5 * time.Minute, ...}) used for all cacheWrap types in rbac.NewService, but each cacheWrap sets its own TTL per Set call (e.g. shortCacheTTL=30s for permDenialCache). This works correctly since TTL is passed per Set, but the underlying LocalCache's global Expiry (5m) could override/compete with per-entry TTLs for cleanup semantics depending on the authlib cache implementation; worth verifying that the authlib LocalCache correctly honors the TTL argument passed to Set rather than relying on the Config.Expiry, since misconfiguration here was not covered by any test added in this PR.

Permission cache not invalidated/refreshed consistently between Check cache-hit and re-fetch paths

When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cache hit but checkPermission returns false (not allowed), the code falls through to re-fetch permissions via getIdentityPermissions and overwrite the perm cache with fresh data (service.go line ~139-155). This means every 'miss' on a stale/incomplete cached scope map triggers a full DB fetch, which is the intended fix, but combined with permDenialCache being set afterward, a legitimate but just-granted permission that arrives between the cached-permission check and the DB fetch could still get cached as a denial if the DB read is also stale (e.g. read replica lag). There's no documentation or handling of eventual consistency behind permissionStore.GetUserPermissions, so denial caching on top of potentially stale reads compounds the staleness window instead of resolving it reliably.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Comment above useAllAlertRuleAbilities refers to its own deprecated usage incorrectly

The comment '// This hook is being called a lot...' was moved under useAllAlertRuleAbilities but it originally described performance concerns for that specific (now deprecated) hook. Since the hook now simply delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, the comment is misleading as placed - it implies the memoization optimization lives directly in this wrapper, but the actual heavy useMemo lives in useAllRulerRuleAbilities, called via delegation on every re-render of groupIdentifierV2 memo dependency on rule, which recomputes a new object identity whenever rule changes, potentially duplicating the concern rather than fixing it.

Delete menu item hidden when rulerRule is absent for Grafana-managed rules from list view

`canDelete` is now computed from either rulerRuleAbility or grafanaPromRuleAbility, but the actual menu rendering condition at `{canDelete && rulerRule && (...)}` still requires `rulerRule` to be truthy. Since the whole point of this PR is to support the case where only `promRule` is available (ruler API removed from list view), delete action will never render for rules coming from the alert list view even when `canDelete` is true via `grafanaDeleteAbility`. `handleDelete` also requires a `RulerRuleDTO` parameter, so the API is inconsistent with the new partial-data flow.

Pause menu item still gated on rulerRule only

The pause menu item condition `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && groupIdentifier.groupOrigin === 'grafana'` requires rulerRule to be a grafana rule, but canPause can now become true purely from grafanaPauseAbility (based on promRule) without rulerRule being present. This means pause will never show in the alert-list-view context even though canPause is true, since MenuItemPauseRule requires a RulerRuleDTO rule prop that isn't present.

Removed ruler rule matching no longer differentiates creating/deleting rule states

The previous implementation fetched both ruler and Prometheus data and used matchRules to render 'Creating' (ruler-only) and 'Deleting' (prom-only) states via RuleOperation. This PR removes the ruler fetch and the matching logic entirely, rendering only Prometheus-sourced rules. As a result the UI will not show rules that exist only in ruler but haven't propagated to Prometheus yet (creating state), nor rules that still appear in Prometheus but were deleted from ruler (deleting state), effectively silently dropping these transitional states without a replacement implementation or test coverage for the removed behavior described by matchRules tests that were deleted.

useRulerRuleAbility called with possibly undefined rule but still used for canEditRule logic unconditionally

useRulerRuleAbility(rule, groupIdentifier, AlertRuleAction.Update) is called even when `rule` is undefined (RuleProps now allows either rule or promRule). While useAllRulerRuleAbilities tolerates undefined rule, mixing this with the new useGrafanaPromRuleAbility fallback obscures intent and risks returning stale/incorrect ability tuples (e.g., when both rule and promRule happen to be present but inconsistent, the OR logic could incorrectly grant edit permission based on whichever path returns true first).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Double interpolation risk when runSplitQuery is called from shardQuerySplitting

runSplitQuery now applies datasource.applyTemplateVariables to each query. However, shardQuerySplitting.ts also calls applyTemplateVariables on queries before invoking runSplitQuery (via runSplitQuery -> runSplitGroupedQueries). This means queries get interpolated twice: once in runShardSplitQuery and again inside runSplitQuery. If applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent (e.g. for variables with special characters, regex escaping, or variables that get consumed/removed on first pass), this could produce corrupted queries or double-escaping, and is wasteful. This also changes order relative to shard selector interpolation (interpolateShardingSelector happens before the second applyTemplateVariables call), which may re-process the shard selector unexpectedly.

Interpolated queries passed into runSplitQuery for re-interpolation

runShardSplitQuery interpolates queries via applyTemplateVariables and passes them to splitQueriesByStreamShard, which eventually calls runSplitQuery with already-interpolated expressions (including shard selector interpolation via interpolateShardingSelector). Since runSplitQuery itself now calls applyTemplateVariables again on its targets, the shard-selector-modified expr (containing __stream_shard__ labels) will be run through applyTemplateVariables a second time. If applyTemplateVariables performs operations that aren't safe to re-apply (e.g., stripping/escaping of variable syntax, or relies on original unmodified expr), this could silently break shard-filtered queries or produce incorrect results that aren't caught by existing tests focused only on happy-path interpolation of $__auto/$step variables.

Loss of per-query metadata/order from applyTemplateVariables map

The new `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters))` is applied to all non-hidden, non-empty queries uniformly, but applyTemplateVariables for sharded/interpolated selector queries previously happened in a different place with different context. No test covers interaction with scopedVars per-query differences (e.g., when `request.filters` is combined with sharding-specific values), so there's a test gap for the combined sharding + ad hoc filter + split scenario.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
traceID log attribute silently dropped

The old logRequest implementation added a 'traceID' attribute (via tracing.TraceIDFromContext) to each log entry. The rewritten logRequest no longer includes traceID, and the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware/contextual_logger_middleware.go also doesn't add it. This means plugin request completion logs will no longer be correlatable with trace IDs, a regression in observability that isn't mentioned in the PR description.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards call context, breaking tests of contextual logging

FromContext on TestLogger always returns a fresh NewTestLogger() instance that has no connection to the original TestLogger's recorded calls or the context's attributes. Since LoggerMiddleware now calls m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...) instead of m.logger.Info(...), any test using TestLogger to assert on logged messages/attributes via LoggerMiddleware will not observe anything recorded on the original TestLogger instance, since the Info call happens on the discarded instance. This silently breaks the ability to unit test LoggerMiddleware's logging behavior with TestLogger, and no updated test was included for logger_middleware.go despite the significant behavior change (contextual attributes, dropped pluginId/endpoint/dsName/uname/traceID in logParams).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Removed structured log fields (pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID, uname) from logParams without equivalent verification

logRequest previously added pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID directly into logParams. These are now expected to come via the contextual logger set by ContextualLoggerMiddleware/instrumentContext, but there's no test verifying that the final emitted log record actually contains these fields through the FromContext()-based logger chain. If the contextual-logger wiring order ever changes (e.g., LoggerMiddleware placed before ContextualLoggerMiddleware), these fields would be silently lost from logs with no test coverage to catch such a regression.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Race condition in device-limit enforcement

CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices and only if count < deviceLimit proceeds with the upsert. Between the count check and the insert there is no locking/transaction, so concurrent requests can all pass the check and insert simultaneously, allowing the device count to exceed deviceLimit. The limit is a soft, racy guard rather than a hard limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Anonymous authentication now fails synchronously when device-tagging fails

Previously TagDevice was invoked asynchronously in a goroutine so tagging failures (including DB errors) never blocked authentication. Now Authenticate calls TagDevice synchronously and returns the error directly (not just for ErrDeviceLimitReached but anything propagated from TagDevice/tagDeviceUI/CreateOrUpdateDevice), which will cause Authenticate to fail and reject anonymous access on any device-tagging error, e.g. transient DB issues, not just when the limit is actually reached. This changes behavior for all non-limit errors from 'warn and continue' to 'fail the request'. Also, running TagDevice synchronously now adds a DB round trip to every anonymous request's auth path, which could have a performance impact that wasn't present before (the removed goroutine had a timeout and panic recovery that are no longer present).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging uses log.Error level

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags use r.log.Error(...) for routine informational logging of counts (e.g. 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time'). This is not an error condition and will pollute error logs/alerting on every cleanup cycle. Should be Debug or Info level.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification

The ticker interval for running all cleanup jobs (including unrelated ones like snapshot/dashboard version/image/query history cleanup) was reduced from every 10 minutes to every 1 minute. This is a 10x increase in frequency for all cleanup jobs, not just annotation cleanup, which could increase load unnecessarily and isn't explained in the PR description, which only discusses deadlock avoidance via query splitting.

false_positives.candidate:
Fetch and delete occur in separate non-transactional statements, allowing race / double counting

fetchIDs and deleteByIDs are now executed as two separate WithDbSession calls without a shared transaction. Between the SELECT and subsequent DELETE, rows matching the condition could be concurrently modified (e.g. tags change, or org cleanup settings elsewhere), causing deletes of IDs that no longer meet the criteria, or missing newly matching rows. The PR documents accepting under-deletion but doesn't address potential over-deletion by ID when a row's content changed between fetch and delete (e.g. an annotation unexpectedly becoming non-matching no longer matters because deletion is by ID only, so any row with that ID gets deleted regardless of current state).

deleteByIDs loses non-SQLite batch deadlock protection by not splitting large ID lists

deleteByIDs builds a single DELETE ... WHERE id IN (...) statement with up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize parameters for non-SQLite databases. For large batch sizes this still issues one large multi-row DELETE statement which can hold locks for an extended period, partially re-introducing the kind of lock contention this PR is trying to avoid, since the fix only addressed the subquery lock scope, not statement size for MySQL under large batch configs.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection records legacy outcome under storage metric

In the DeleteCollection async goroutine, after calling d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`, mislabeling the legacy write duration/outcome as a storage metric.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records metric using resource name instead of kind

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes `name` (the object's name) where other calls pass `options.Kind`. This produces inconsistent/incorrect metric labels, mixing up object names and resource kinds across metrics, making dashboards for mode3 delete duration unreliable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Fire-and-forget goroutines use parent context that may be canceled before legacy write completes

In Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection, the async goroutine does `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` deriving from the request's ctx. Once the HTTP request completes, the original ctx is typically canceled by the server, which will immediately cancel the derived context too, aborting the legacy write before the 10s timeout is reached. This defeats the purpose of "asynchronously write to legacy as a safe measure" since most async legacy writes will likely be canceled right after the response is sent back to the client, silently dropping legacy writes.

Metric mislabeled as legacy duration on storage failure

In Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` — but this is a storage failure, not a legacy failure. This mislabels the metric, polluting legacy error-duration metrics with storage errors. The same pattern repeats in Update (line ~129) where a storage failure is recorded via `recordLegacyDuration`.

No test coverage for async legacy writes

The new tests for Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection only assert the result returned from Storage; they never assert that the legacy store's Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection mocks were actually called (there's no `AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` on the legacy mock, and goroutines are fire-and-forget with no synchronization), so the core new behavior of mode 3 — asynchronously writing to legacy as a safety measure — is effectively untested and could silently regress.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false, inverted logic also present

The function enableSqlExpressions computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (i.e. enabled is true when the flag is NOT enabled), then returns false either way (both branches return false). This makes the function always return false regardless of feature flag state, meaning SQL expressions are unconditionally disabled even when intentionally wanted, and the logic is nonsensical/dead code. While this currently achieves the goal of disabling the vulnerable feature, the naming and logic are backwards and misleading, and if flag intent is ever restored this will silently remain broken. Should be a simple hard return false with a clear comment, or fixed boolean logic tied to the feature flag.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TablesList calls RunCommands which always errors, breaking valid SQL expression configs

db.go's RunCommands (and QueryFramesInto) stub always returns errors.New("not implemented"). TablesList calls duckDB.RunCommands and will always fail, so even when FlagSqlExpressions were enabled in future, any SQL expression would fail with 'error serializing sql: not implemented'. There's no test covering TablesList/QueryFramesInto behavior change, so broken functionality isn't caught in CI.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests updated/added for disabled SQL execution path

The PR disables the DuckDB-backed SQL engine by stubbing it out, but no tests were added or updated to verify that SQLCommand.Execute now fails gracefully, or that ReadQuery rejects QueryTypeSQL properly in all code paths (e.g., UnmarshalSQLCommand doesn't check the feature flag at all, so legacy/alerting code paths that call UnmarshalSQLCommand directly bypass the ReadQuery-level block and will reach the broken Execute path silently).

UnmarshalSQLCommand does not check feature flag / enablement before constructing command

UnmarshalSQLCommand (used for legacy raw-node parsing, e.g. in alerting) builds a SQLCommand without any check against enableSqlExpressions or the FlagSqlExpressions toggle, unlike ReadQuery which blocks QueryTypeSQL. This means code paths that use UnmarshalSQLCommand instead of ReadQuery could still attempt to construct and execute SQL commands, which only fail later via the stubbed db.go (and only because of that side effect), rather than being explicitly disabled. This is fragile: if db.go stub is removed/replaced in future without restoring the check here, the vulnerable code path reopens silently.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Finer-grained locking introduces race for concurrent BuildIndex calls on the same key

GetIndex uses cacheMu.RLock to check the cache, and BuildIndex no longer holds a lock for the whole build process (previously the full function was locked). Now, two concurrent calls to getOrCreateIndex for the same NamespacedResource (e.g., during Search or handleEvent when the index doesn't exist yet) can race: both see nil from GetIndex, and both proceed to independently build full indexes for the same key before only one of their results survives in `cache[key]` (last writer wins) — wasting resources and potentially leaving a stale/duplicate bleve.Index handle (and underlying directory bleve.New(dir,...) for file-based ones) open and never closed, leaking file handles/goroutines.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Init uses sync.Once — a transient failure permanently blocks the server

s.once.Do caches the first result in s.initErr; if Init fails once (e.g., due to a transient index/watcher error), every future caller of Init will get the same cached error forever since Once never re-runs. Since Init is now called once at construction and no longer called before every RPC, this effectively means a single early failure can never be recovered without restarting the whole process. Previously, each RPC re-called Init, giving many chances to succeed; now there's exactly one attempt with no retry path at all, since RPC handlers no longer call Init themselves.

NewResourceServer now blocks startup synchronously and can fail hard on index build errors

Init(ctx) is now called synchronously inside NewResourceServer, using the long-lived background ctx (claims.WithClaims(context.Background())). Any transient failure during search index build (e.g. slow DB, timeout, or temporary storage issue) now causes NewResourceServer to return an error, which can prevent the whole module/server from starting. Previously, failures were deferred to first gRPC call and could be retried per-request. This is a behavior/API change that could turn transient indexing problems into full startup failures, with no retry mechanism.

Removed guard against unitialized server: RPCs no longer check Init before executing

All gRPC handlers (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, PutBlob, GetBlob) previously called s.Init(ctx) defensively before executing; this diff removes all of those calls, relying solely on the one-time Init call during NewResourceServer. If NewResourceServer's Init silently failed in a way that returned a server anyway, or if some other code path constructs `server` without going through NewResourceServer (e.g., tests), these methods will now run against a server where backend/watcher weren't properly initialized, with no safety net or explicit error returned.

Watch loop ignores context cancellation, can leak goroutine with init's background context

s.search.init starts a goroutine using watchctx := context.Background() reading from `events` in an infinite for loop with no select on ctx.Done(). Since init is now called synchronously during server construction with its own context (that is subsequently discarded, since watchctx is a new unrelated background context), there is no way to ever stop this goroutine except for the channel closing. Combined with the search support being created once per ResourceServer and that now being constructed eagerly at startup, any server restart/shutdown path that doesn't close the `events` channel will leak this goroutine indefinitely.

false_positives.candidate:
getForLogin cache key does not depend on organizationId for ORG_ONLY/ALL modes

cacheKeyForLogin only incorporates the FetchMode, not the organizationId, but the underlying IdentityProviderListQuery stores results per searchKey (organizationId) within that single cached entry. This means a single invalidation key is shared across all organizationId values for a given mode, which is fine for invalidation but means the cache entry for FetchMode.ORG_ONLY/ALL grows unbounded as more distinct organizationIds are queried (there is no eviction except full invalidation), since IdentityProviderListQuery accumulates entries per searchKey indefinitely until the whole object is invalidated. This can lead to unbounded memory growth in deployments with many organizations repeatedly queried under FetchMode.ALL/ORG_ONLY.

getLoginPredicate() missing null-safety for idp.getConfig()

The predicate added at line 254 calls idp.getConfig().get(...) without checking if getConfig() can return null. If an IdentityProviderModel exists with a null config map, this will throw a NullPointerException when evaluating login eligibility, breaking getForLogin and all cache paths that rely on this predicate (create, remove, update invalidation logic).

remove() invalidates login caches even when IDP is unknown

In remove(), storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) can be null if the alias doesn't exist. registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp) is then called with a null idp, which calls getLoginPredicate().test(null). The predicate starts with Objects::nonNull so it returns false safely, but this relies on implicit behavior rather than an explicit null check, making the code fragile to future predicate reordering and obscuring intent.

update() invalidation ordering depends on stale idpById before delegate update

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(idpById, model) is called using idpById (the pre-update state fetched via getById, potentially from cache) and the new model, before idpDelegate.update(model) is executed. If getById returned a stale cached entry whose login-eligibility differs from the actual DB state, the invalidation decision could be made on outdated data, potentially skipping a needed cache invalidation when organizationId or other login fields have changed outside of this fetch's visibility (e.g., concurrent updates).

true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider misleadingly returns the default KeyStore provider

getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is not actually the BouncyCastle provider in most environments (it's whatever the default KeyStore provider is, e.g. SUN). This is semantically wrong for a method whose contract is to return a BouncyCastle-based security provider, and any caller relying on getBouncyCastleProvider() to get BC capabilities will get an unrelated provider, potentially causing subtle failures or wrong algorithm lookups downstream.

false_positives.candidate:
CryptoIntegration.init called without checking for pre-existing/conflicting provider

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). If the authz-client is used within the main Keycloak server or testsuite (sharing a classloader where both the AuthzClientCryptoProvider and DefaultCryptoProvider service files are visible), detectProvider will pick whichever has higher order (DefaultCryptoProvider order=200 > AuthzClientCryptoProvider order=100), but since CryptoIntegration.init is a once-only init guarded by a null check, if some other code path already initialized CryptoIntegration with a different provider before AuthzClient.create is called, this call becomes a no-op, silently keeping the previous provider. This ordering/initialization-order dependency is fragile and not well documented; combined with the lack of multiple-provider detection warnings, it can result in using the wrong CryptoProvider in mixed classpath scenarios without any error.

Removed safety check allows silent selection among multiple CryptoProviders

The previous behavior threw an IllegalStateException when multiple CryptoProvider implementations were found on the classpath, forcing developers to notice and resolve ambiguous crypto configurations. This PR replaces that with silent ordering/sorting by order(), picking the highest order and merely logging (at debug level) which providers were ignored. If a deployment accidentally has two crypto providers on the classpath (e.g. due to a dependency misconfiguration), it will silently pick one based on order value instead of failing fast, which could lead to the wrong crypto provider being used in production without any visible warning (debug logging is typically disabled).

getClientsWithPermission iterates resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) and adds resource.getName() to the granted set. This will also include the pseudo resource named after CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE itself (the 'all-clients' resource), which is not an actual client ID. Callers treating the returned set as a list of real client IDs could get a bogus entry equal to the resource type name, causing invalid downstream behavior (e.g. attempting to look up a client with id 'Clients').

The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. false_positives.candidate:
Inconsistent resource lookup key for all-clients permission check

In hasPermission(String scope) the all-clients resource is looked up via resourceStore.findByName(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, server.getId()), while hasPermission(ClientModel, String) uses AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...) to resolve the same 'all-clients' resource. Using two different lookup paths for what should be the same resource is fragile; if the resource type name differs from the resource name convention used elsewhere, this method will silently return false even when an all-clients permission exists, since it doesn't fall back to resolving via getResourceTypeResource like the other overload does.

No fallback when resource.getScopes() doesn't include the needed scope semantics

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), when the specific client resource exists, it is evaluated directly without checking whether an 'all-clients' permission could still grant extra permissions beyond what's modeled for the single resource (e.g. a MANAGE permission on all-clients should also grant VIEW/CONFIGURE even if the specific client resource only has a narrower permission). This differs from canManage()/canView() combos elsewhere that explicitly call multiple canX() methods for transitive scope checks, but hasPermission by itself does not combine both the specific-resource and all-resource evaluations, potentially under-granting access when both exist with different scopes.

Changing RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE breaks documented/scripted exit codes

This changes the exit code contract documented in update-compatibility.adoc and relied on by external scripts/CI pipelines. false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. false_positives.candidate:
Removed grantIfNoPermission fallback changes semantics for canQuery/canView ordering

canQuery() now calls root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.QUERY_USERS) || canView() instead of previously checking canView() first then QUERY_USERS role; order change is harmless for boolean OR, but note canManageDefault/canViewDefault helper methods used by canManageByGroup/canViewByGroup chains across GroupPermissions were removed/inlined without an accompanying check that all V1 fallback call sites (e.g., RolePermissions.canMapRole) still behave identically. Given RolePermissions.canMapRole previously called root.users().canManageDefault() and now calls root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS) directly, any custom logic inside canManageDefault() beyond the role check (if present in other code paths or overridden in subclasses) is now bypassed. This refactor should be verified for all previous callers of the removed canManageDefault/canViewDefault helpers to ensure no behavior regressed, especially for V1 class hierarchies that might have relied on virtual dispatch of these methods.

canManage(UserModel) role check changed from ADMIN+MANAGE_USERS to only MANAGE_USERS

The diff removes AdminRoles.ADMIN from the hasOneAdminRole() check in canView(UserModel) and canManage(UserModel). This could change authorization behavior for callers previously granted access via the generic ADMIN role; if ADMIN role holders are expected to always have access, this is a regression that should be confirmed as intentional (schema cleanup) and covered by a test.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission only checks root.users().canView(), ignoring canManage()

Previously (per the diff), the old getGroupsWithViewPermission() method checked both canView() and canManage() of root.users() before returning empty set. The new getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() only checks root.users().canView(). This means an admin with only manage permission on users (but not explicit view) will now have groups incorrectly filtered/computed, which could result in incorrect scoping or performance overhead from needlessly computing group IDs when the admin should already have full access via manage permission.

searchForUser no longer checks canView() before computing/filtering groupIds, double filtering removed

The old code wrapped the groupIds lookup in `if (!auth.users().canView())`, avoiding unnecessary computation of group IDs for admins who can already view all users, and separately filtered the stream with `.filter(usersEvaluator::canView)`. The new code unconditionally computes `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` (which internally checks canView() so it's not functionally broken) and removes the `.filter(usersEvaluator::canView)` on the stream from `searchForUserStream`, instead relying solely on `toRepresentation`'s filter. This refactor is likely fine functionally, but removing the direct filtering here is a behavior-sensitive change that should be covered by tests ensuring per-user permission filtering still works correctly when group-based attribute injection (UserModel.GROUPS session attribute) is used with searchForUserStream, since the underlying store query uses the GROUPS session attribute for filtering, and if that store-level filtering has gaps, results could leak un-permitted users without an additional in-memory filter safety net.

false_positives.candidate:
English reference file lookup is fragile and may throw unhandled exceptions

`verifySafeHtml` derives the English reference file path by naively doing `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`. If a path contains "resources-community" multiple times, or the filename pattern doesn't match (e.g. en file itself, or a locale name containing unexpected characters), this can produce an incorrect path. More importantly, if the computed `englishFile` doesn't exist (e.g. missing en counterpart for a given theme/module), `new FileInputStream(englishFile)` throws FileNotFoundException, which is wrapped as an unchecked `RuntimeException` propagated out of `verify()`, which only declares `MojoExecutionException`. This will crash the whole build for any file without a matching English counterpart rather than reporting a soft validation failure.

normalizeValue hardcodes key-specific exceptions reducing maintainability/generality

normalizeValue special-cases specific keys ("templateHelp", "optimizeLookupHelp", keys starting with "linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit", or "error-invalid-multivalued-size") directly in the verifier logic instead of deriving these exceptions from data/config. Any new translation key introducing legitimate special syntax (e.g., new choice-format messages or generic placeholders resembling HTML tags) will trigger false-positive 'Illegal HTML' failures until the verifier code itself is updated, creating ongoing maintenance burden tied to translation content changes rather than to code changes.

santizeAnchors uses replaceFirst on whole string potentially matching wrong occurrence

`santizeAnchors` iterates anchor tags found via the matcher, but calls `value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")` against the *original* `value` string on each loop iteration, not the updated local variable's position context. If the same anchor tag string appears multiple times in `value`, repeated calls to `replaceFirst` with the same pattern will always remove the first occurrence, never advancing past already-processed matches, potentially stripping the wrong occurrence or looping incorrectly relative to `matcher`'s cursor (which continues scanning the original `value`, not the mutated one), causing find/replace to get out of sync and produce incorrect sanitized results or false positive 'anchor mismatch' messages.

verify() swallows RuntimeExceptions raised deep in verifySafeHtml without proper MojoExecutionException wrapping

`verify()` catches only `IOException` around `verifySafeHtml()`, but `verifySafeHtml()` internally throws unchecked `RuntimeException` (for FileNotFoundException-like issues) rather than IOException. These RuntimeExceptions will propagate uncaught out of `verify()`, breaking the stated `throws MojoExecutionException` contract and potentially causing an unhandled build failure with a less helpful stack trace instead of a clean MojoExecutionException.

Wrong variable null-checked for rawTokenId

In the constructor, `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` checks `grantType` again instead of `rawTokenId`. As a result, a null `rawTokenId` will not be caught here, potentially leading to NPEs later when `rawTokenId` is used (e.g., string concatenation producing "null" instead of failing fast).

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher logic inverted

The matchesSafely method returns false when the actual grant shortcut equals the expected shortcut: `if (items[0].substring(3,5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. This inverts the intended check — it should return false (fail) when the shortcut does NOT match, but as written it fails precisely when it matches and otherwise falls through to return true even for wrong shortcuts. This means tests using isAccessTokenId effectively never properly validate the grant type shortcut and will reject the correct token IDs, causing false test failures or false negatives (letting incorrect token IDs pass undetected).

false_positives.candidate:
Access token ID format changed, breaking consumers that assume raw UUID token IDs

Token IDs are now encoded with a 6-character context prefix followed by ':' and the raw UUID (e.g. `onrtac:1f65761e-...`). Any external or internal code/tests that previously assumed access token 'jti'/id is a plain UUID (e.g. length 36, UUID format validations, log parsing, DB lookups keyed by token id) will break. The PR already needed to update AssertEvents' isUUID-based matchers for this reason, indicating this is a breaking format change that should be clearly called out as such for downstream integrations relying on jti format.

Hardcoded refresh grant type note set unconditionally on token refresh/validation path

In validateToken, `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN);` is set unconditionally whenever a token is being recreated/validated. This overwrites whatever grant type was originally used to create the client session context (e.g., authorization_code, device_code, ciba), even when this path is invoked for scenarios other than classic refresh-token grant (e.g. offline token refresh paths reused elsewhere), causing the encoded token ID's grant-type shortcut to incorrectly always read as 'rt' instead of the actual originating grant, undermining the stated purpose of the feature (correctly identifying grant type from the token ID).

Non-atomic cache refresh for grant type shortcuts can race under concurrent token issuance

getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut perform read-then-conditionally-write operations on ConcurrentHashMap without synchronization across the two maps (grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts). Although ConcurrentHashMap operations are individually thread-safe, the two maps can become inconsistent between each other under concurrent provider deployment/refresh scenarios, and the duplicate-shortcut validation done once in postInit is not re-run during runtime cache refresh, so a newly deployed grant type with a shortcut colliding with an existing one would silently overwrite entries without the earlier safety check that aborts startup.

generatedCodesString, generatedAtTimeString, and generatedUserLabel are read from form parameters without null checks before being used in generatedAtTimeString.equals(...) and Long.valueOf(generatedAtTimeString). If an attacker/misbehaving client submits the required action without these hidden fields, this throws NPE/NumberFormatException instead of being handled gracefully, which existed before but is still unaddressed by this change that otherwise reworks the flow.

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only validates login with the first recovery code (index 0) stored in the federated/user-storage provider. updateCredential return value used ambiguously to detect userStorage success

This mirrors the same questionable pattern already used for OTP but duplicates the ambiguity for a new credential type without additional safety checks (e.g. verifying supportsCredentialType first), risking silently creating duplicate or no credential in edge-case federated providers.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offset slicing produces invalid/undefined queryset behavior

When `self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing/slicing (unlike Python lists) and will raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` at runtime. No tests added for new OptimizedCursorPaginator

The PR adds an entirely new paginator class (OptimizedCursorPaginator) with non-trivial new behavior (negative offset handling, enable_advanced_features flag) but includes no unit tests. Given the negative-offset slicing bug and altered trimming logic, this lack of test coverage means the regression would not be caught before release.
